-> **HERMETIC PHILOSOPHY** <-
<note>original Latin: *PHILOSOPHIA HERMETICA*. This refers to a tradition of esoteric wisdom, alchemy, and spiritual transformation attributed to the legendary figure Hermes Trismegistus.</note>

**[An intricate circular emblem is centered on the page:]**

The outer border of the emblem is formed by a green **Ouroboros**—a serpent biting its own tail—symbolizing eternity, the unity of the beginning and the end, and the cyclical nature of the universe. Inside this circle, the words "**HERMETIC PHILOSOPHY**" are inscribed.

Within the center of the emblem, set against a blue sky, a **golden sun** shines with rays reaching downward. Below the sun, a **white pelican** is depicted in her nest, pecking her own breast to feed her young with her blood. This motif, known as the **"pelican in her piety,"** is a classic symbol of self-sacrifice and, in an alchemical context, represents the stage of the "Great Work" where the substance is nourished and perfected.

The nest rests atop a **white cube**, which represents the physical world or the "salt" of the philosophers. On the front face of this cube, two **golden staves** are crossed diagonally, with **four red roses** placed at the top, bottom, left, and right of the intersection—a hallmark of **Rosicrucian** <term>Rosicrucian: a secret philosophical society of the 17th century that used the Rose and Cross as symbols of spiritual unfolding</term> iconography.

<summary>This is the title page of a manuscript on Hermetic Philosophy, featuring a rich alchemical emblem that combines symbols of eternity, sacrifice, and Rosicrucian mysticism.</summary>

# ANNOTATIONS 
# ON THE WALDENSIAN
# CONFESSION, REGARDING THE CHAPTERS
### that differ from the Augsburg Confession,
<note>The Augsburg Confession (1530) was the primary statement of faith for the Lutheran movement. This book examines where the "Waldensian" faith—an older medieval reform movement—diverged from Lutheranism.</note>

## THE RESPONSE
## PUBLISHED SOME TIME AGO,
### in the name of the Bohemian

This same writing of mine, before and around the time of its publication, was subjected to the judgment of certain Magnificent Lords and more eminent Theologians and Pastors, who were performing their duties both among the Bohemians (with whom the Brethren share a common homeland) and among the Germans. Therefore, when this little work of mine—at the urging of many, and especially through a certain heroic impulse and at the expense of the Magnificent Lord John Spanoffsky <note>Jan Špánovský z Lisova (c. 1540–1591), a prominent Protestant nobleman in Bohemia</note>, the Elder, of Lisau in Pacov <note>original: "Lyſau in Patzauo"; a town in the Pelhřimov District of the Czech Republic</note>, to whom may it be well forever—had been printed once, rumors were spread everywhere concerning a "Response" prepared by the Bohemian Brethren <note>The Unitas Fratrum, a pre-Reformation Christian denomination in the Kingdom of Bohemia</note> against it. Among others, the author of this response was said to be, on account of his style, a certain Sacramentarian <term>Sacramentarian: a derogatory term used by Lutherans for those (often Calvinists or followers of Zwingli) who denied the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist, viewing the bread and wine as mere symbols</term>. This man was not a theologian by profession, but a philosopher, who, as a fugitive from Saxony, had shortly before given his name to the Waldensian society <note>The author refers to the Bohemian Brethren as "Waldensians," a common polemical tactic to link them to an older medieval sect</note>, as he held the same views as they did.

But neither I, nor others devoted to our Confession <note>The Augsburg Confession, the defining document of Lutheranism</note> then living in that same province of Moravia, happened to see anything of the sort that had been set against my book (as far as I know). Furthermore, public rumor later added that it would happen at another time—namely after my death, and when all copies of my little book had already been dispersed—that this Response would be published. This was supposedly planned so that my words would no longer be compared with their response, nor would timely testimony be offered for the truth as it struggled, nor could the various slanders inserted into that same Response be openly countered. I argued that the peace of CHRIST and the Divine Spirit must be valued more highly than civil and external peace.

-># PREFACE <-

I had already decided—unless something similar or even more bitter were to be thrust upon me—that amidst the perpetual occupations of my duties and studies, and in my now advancing age, I would not dispute further about these many matters, but would leave them to others. This was especially so because it seemed to me, and to many good men, that a certain satisfaction had been reached. I felt that the opportunity for the Waldensian Ministers <note>The "Waldensian Ministers" here refers to the Bohemian Brethren, a pre-Reformation Christian group that the author views as theological rivals who were drawing members away from the established Lutheran churches.</note> to alienate more people from our Churches in the future and draw them into their own society had been, in some way, cut off—as the situation itself has shown in various places, and especially in the neighboring Church then entrusted to me.

Nor do I add much regarding the fact that I had allowed myself to be persuaded that not everything had been inserted into their Confessions by deliberate choice and after careful consideration <note>original: "ἐκ προαιρέσεως καὶ περιεσκεμμένως"</note>, but rather thoughtlessly and without foresight <note>original: "ἀπρονοήτως καὶ ἀπερισκέπτως"</note>, or that their actions against us and our Churches until now were perhaps unintentional. For this reason, I judged that I should yield to the times, hoping that if both sides remained quiet, it might eventually happen that they would correct certain things of their own accord. I hoped that—following the holy advice of Dr. Luther <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the leader of the German Reformation.</note>, or rather the command of the Apostle himself in 1 Corinthians 1:10 <note>This verse reads: "I appeal to you, brothers and sisters, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree with one another in what you say and that there be no divisions among you..."</note>—if they did not wish for there to be fewer schisms <term>Schism: A formal split or division within a religious body.</term>, they might at least administer their affairs more cautiously in the future by straying less from the path.

But truly, to the most Merciful GOD, who is aware of all things, and who at last brings into the light <note>original: "in apricum profert"; a Latin idiom meaning to bring something out into the sunshine or to make it public.</note> both well-done and ill-done deeds, and the truth not at all...

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of the "Brothers" (the Bohemian Brethren). -># PREFACE <-

...it is not without danger to live among those who oppose their errors and injustices. Indeed, this venerable man writes that he has suffered much at their hands in various places—though, as with all other accusations, they completely deny this one as well. Furthermore, one can see from this that they deceptively <note>original: "ἀπατηλῶς" (apatēlos)</note> hide their defensive writings and commentaries—in which they attempt to champion their own inventions and those of their ancestors. Or, at the very least, they share them privately only with those they know are indebted to them. They do this so that the opportunity for a timely and fair rebuttal might be denied to those whom it concerns most, across all parties.

Consequently, it required extraordinary skill to obtain the copy of the *Response* <note>Referring to the secret document written by the Bohemian Brethren to counter the author’s previous criticisms.</note> that was sent to me. It likely would never have been secured had it not been for an uncertain rumor that was circulating at the time: a report that I had died during the outbreak of the plague <note>original: "pestis"</note> in the town of Helmstedt <note>A prominent university town in Lower Saxony, Germany, where the author, likely David Chytraeus, was a professor.</note>. 

As for the reason they give for why this document has not been published until now—namely, their claim that they feared I would use the opportunity to attack them with even more writings—they certainly had no reason to fear. That is, if they had approached the matter with proper moderation; if, amidst so many monstrous errors, they had shown themselves to be teachable and open to correction; and if they had relied on truth rather than falsehood, on the weight of their arguments rather than the vanity of various fictions, and on gentleness rather than bitter insults—a moderation they promised in words but failed to deliver in practice...

In Appendix Notes 1 and 7: They claim that Luther submitted himself without any reservation to the judgment of the Waldensians, and that he changed, corrected, or even fundamentally removed everything he had said more harshly against them. 
<note>The Waldensians were a medieval Christian movement that Martin Luther and other Reformers initially viewed with suspicion but later sought to find common ground with as "pre-Reformation" allies.</note>

In Note 13: Since each of these points, and many others, are entirely alien to the truth—and since I am conscious that these matters are far otherwise, by **GOD'S** grace—I could no longer ignore them or seem to approve of them through silence. 

However, those who judge rightly will easily understand for themselves—once a comparison is made with my previous writing—that such slanders and trifles have proceeded from nothing but notable malice, hostile hatred, and a vehement desire for hurling insults in their <term>Replies</term>.
<note>original: "Respondentibus"; in the context of academic disputations, these were the formal written answers or rebuttals provided by his opponents.</note>

# FROM THE PREFACE
## OF THE RESPONSE
### REMARKS.

First. From the beginning and very frequently thereafter, they <note>Referring to the "Antagonists" or Bohemian Brethren mentioned previously.</note> claim a desire for peace and cite the command of the Apostle <note>Likely referring to Saint Paul’s exhortations to live peaceably, such as in Romans 12:18.</note> to that effect. They add that, for this reason, they have so far been unwilling to respond to several writings published against them. However, they judge peace and charity according to worldly feelings and decide on them in a political manner <note>The author suggests they are playing politics rather than following true spiritual principles.</note>. They fail to observe the extent to which peace should be maintained—namely, that truth must be placed far above it. This is according to the divine command in Zechariah 8:19 <note>The original text cites verse 20, but the command to "love truth and peace" is in verse 19.</note> and Ephesians 4:15. What kind of peace, therefore, can or should be rightly held when it coincides with the scattering and oppression of heavenly truth, the glory of GOD, and His <term>orthodox</term> <note>From the Greek *orthos* (right) and *doxa* (belief); the author uses this to describe his own "correct" faith against the opponents' views.</note> Church in these lands? Therefore, my Respondents must take great care lest they be among those of whom JEHOVAH most gravely complains through Ezekiel in chapter 13, verse 10, for deceiving His people by saying, "Peace, peace," when there is no peace, etc. To this I add the saying of Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his defense of Trinitarian theology.</note>: *War is more praiseworthy than that peace which separates us from GOD.* <note>original: "Laudabilius est bellum, quàm pax ea, quæ nos à DEO disiungit."</note>

II. They write that they have long since rendered an account of their faith and religion, simply and candidly, according to the precept of Saint Peter <note>Referring to 1 Peter 3:15: "Always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that you have."</note>, etc. On the contrary, [they have failed] in just simplicity and candor,

Thus, by their segregation, they provide an occasion for public scandal to others.

### NOTES ###

...the **Confession** regarding the **Sacramentarian** <term>Sacramentarian: A term used at the time to describe those who held a symbolic view of the Eucharist (like the followers of Zwingli or Calvin), which was a major point of contention between different Protestant groups.</term> matter is clearly detected from Articles VIII, XIII, XIV, and XV of this document.

XV. They add that a *gracious response to everything* <note>original: "Benignum ad omnia responsum"</note> was received from the *Most Clement Emperor* <note>Referring to Maximilian II, who reigned until 1576.</note>. Truly, regarding the *Waldensian Confession* (for I am speaking of this at least, and not of other Acts of these Diets), the opposite is proved by a most severe Edict promulgated shortly after in that same year, 1575, by his *Imperial Majesty* in the city of **Speyer**, concerning the suppression and cessation of the separate religion, sermons, and *Waldensian* meetings and secret assemblies. This same edict was subsequently repeated and publicly promulgated by the *Most Invincible Emperor Rudolph II in Prague* in the year 1584.

Therefore, let my respondents see to it that they do not become the authors and agents of many calamities for themselves and their own people (which they perversely blame on me here), since they might be the reason that an inquiry is made into them, rather than me: specifically, whether they are guilty of a breach of faith, and whether in this way they burn a shameful mark of infamy upon their own people and provide the magistrate with reasons for far too many necessary tasks and occupations. ### XVIII. 
They return to the claim *that everything ought to be better understood, and that one should have spoken calmly with them.* But in **Brief Notation XI**, the reasons have already been set forth as to why it would not have been worth the effort to confer with them privately, since others before me performed that task with great care and, as the saying goes, "wasted their oil and labor" <note>original: "oleum... et operam perdiderint"; a Latin idiom meaning to work hard for no result.</note>. ...barbarous <note>This completes the word "barbarous" (Latin: *barbaris*) from the previous page.</note> activities. The author respects Hus as a martyr while critiquing his theological limits.</note>, but for the sake of the comparison established with the light of the **Evangelical doctrine** <term>Evangelical doctrine</term> <note>original: Evangelicæ doctrinæ; a term used by Reformers to describe their theology, which they believed returned to the "Good News" (Gospel) of the New Testament.</note>, which in our times has shone forth more fully and abundantly than it did in the age of Hus. Therefore, I never wished to boast about them "with full cheeks" <note>original: plenis buccis; a Latin idiom meaning to speak pompously, loudly, or with excessive pride.</note>, as my antagonists here falsely claim. As for their claim that struggles and brawls were never to their liking: they ought to consider that such things should not only be avoided, but no occasion for them should be provided. That they have provided such occasions until now is more than manifest in the provinces where they reside.

But I neither prefer Luther to Holy Scripture, nor do I prefer him over any other... <note>The text breaks here; the word "other" (Latin: *quos-*) would be completed as "anyone else" (*quosvis*) on the following page.</note>

# ON THE FIRST PART

This view is condemned—and not without cause—along with other delusions of the fanatics (some of which the Waldensians <note>A medieval movement that sought a return to Apostolic poverty and simplicity; by the time of the Reformation, they were often compared to the Anabaptists or other radical groups by their critics.</note> share with them) in the **Book of Concord** <note>The foundational collection of documents expressing the Lutheran faith, published in 1580.</note>.

They seek empty glory from these things, even though neither they themselves nor the people are readily and willingly subject to them. 

For it is evident that they do not conduct themselves in all things as the Holy Scriptures teach; this is clear from the fact that they confuse the unique calling of the Apostles—to whom the power of teaching everywhere was mandated—with the common calling of other ministers, who are to administer sacred things in one specific place. 

Likewise, in many articles of doctrine, they stubbornly defend corruptions that clearly conflict with the Word of God, despite so many warnings and even the decrees of Synods. Now, because they maintain things contrary to the Holy Scriptures in the most fundamental points, they boast in vain of their mutual consensus, and the discipline and order which they observe in external matters. ...at that time they insisted, in the Response of Jan Blahoslav <note>Jan Blahoslav (1523–1571) was a prominent bishop of the Unity of the Brethren, a humanist scholar, and a key figure in the Bohemian Reformation.</note>, written in the name of the entire society, concerning the Question: *Why the Brethren are separated from other unions [of churches] under one or under both kinds* <note>This refers to the Utraquist tradition of receiving the Eucharist in both "kinds"—bread and wine—a defining issue of the Hussite and Bohemian Reformations.</note>, etc. A similar Response, written in the year 1566 by the Elders of the Unity of the Brethren in Moravia to the Illustrious Count John Frederick <note>John Frederick II, Duke of Saxony (1529–1595), who was a supporter of the Lutheran cause.</note> of pious memory, was presented to me when he summoned me to him at the castle of Kunštát <note>original: *arcem Cunstadianam*; Kunštát is a town in the South Moravian Region of the Czech Republic.</note> in the year 1577.

As for the "Agreement in Poland" <note>This refers to the Consensus of Sandomierz (1570), an important ecumenical agreement between Lutherans, Calvinists, and the Bohemian Brethren in Poland to present a united front.</note> which they mention here—which was entered into between three diverse and opposing Confessions: the **Augsburg** [Lutheran], the **Waldensian** (which they call **Bohemian**), and the **Helvetic** [Reformed/Calvinist]—one may see what the more sincere theologians in Germany judge of it in the "History of the Augsburg Confession" written by them. Whether, indeed, any agreement regarding the Confession was also entered into by them with the Estates of the Kingdom in the Diet of the year 1575, has been shown in Note XIV and XV regarding the Preface.

XVIII. They cite my words, from the chapter on **discipline**, by which—even if they do so unwillingly—they bear witness for me that the pursuit of discipline in the Church committed to my care was by no means neglected. This stands in opposition to the outcries of those men and others who unjustly insult the Ministers of our Churches, as if they had cast off all care for discipline and were accustomed to turn a blind eye to manifest crimes perpetrated against both tables of the **Decalogue** <note>The Ten Commandments, traditionally divided into two "tables": the first four concerning duties to God, and the remaining six concerning duties to one's neighbor.</note>. Moreover, they are mistaken *that they think in that Church, this had not even begun to be enacted*, when in reality, at that very time, it was so maintained that I could testify to it with many examples. 

Thus, the **Antagonists** themselves review one of these examples below—though in very bad faith—in which a funeral procession <note>original: *deductio funebris*; a formal public procession to the grave, which was a mark of social and ecclesiastical standing.</note> was denied (though not the burial or the homeland soil), not to the deceased himself, but to his father, who was a seducer and a deserter of my Church, since he had been a public stumbling block to the whole Church for many years, etc. At that time, even certain individuals who held no small authority in that Republic <note>Likely referring to the civil administration or the state of Bohemia/Moravia.</note> voluntarily submitted themselves to **Ecclesiastical discipline** to consult their own consciences and so that they might receive greater consolation. But whether the discipline of the **Waldensians** <note>A name often applied by outsiders to the Unity of the Brethren (Unitas Fratrum), connecting them to the older medieval reform movement.</note>, which they boast has been proven by long usage, matches the order and example of the primitive Church, is a matter many contend, and the **lawsuit is still before the Judge** <note>original: *sub Iudice lis est*; a Latin idiom meaning the matter is still undecided or under active debate.</note>.

### ON THE FIRST PART

->this very same thing is testified to by the matter itself,<-

concerning the *Response* <note>original: *Responsione*; a specific polemical rebuttal written by the Brethren against the author</note>, compiled against me in the worst of faith. It was printed many years ago, yet for a very long time it was not published at all, but instead kept in darkness and reserved secretly for the uses of that society. This was done so that finally, after my death—when perhaps no one would be defending my just cause or that of our churches as it had been begun—they could thrust it openly upon everyone. 

Dr. Luther <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the primary figure of the Protestant Reformation</note> certainly sensed this same thing long ago when he judged that these Brethren keep their faith captive in their own language, since they profess to believe one thing with their mouths while their published writings say another. Because of this, they twist and interpret sentences of this kind—originally set down with an ambiguous meaning—differently when they are in the presence of our people. # NOTES.

In our time, the Sacramentarians <term>Sacramentarians: a term used by Lutherans for reformers like Zwingli or Calvin, who they believed reduced the bread and wine to mere symbols</term> contend for a purely "spiritual" presence. They set this in opposition not only to a sensible and fleshly presence, but even to the true and substantial body of Christ, denying that His body is present here on earth in the bread of the Holy Supper. Because of this, those phrases used by the ancient Church fathers were brought back into use in the *Apology of the Confession* <note>original: *Apologia Confessionis*; a foundational Lutheran document written by Philipp Melanchthon in 1531 to defend the Augsburg Confession</note> and other writings. This was done to demonstrate that the body of Christ is present in the Supper celebrated here on earth not only in terms of its power and efficacy, but also according to its very substance. It shows that Christ is communicated to us not only spiritually through faith, but also "bodily"—which is to say, the very substance of His body is given in the Holy Supper.

Since these points are clear and evident, we are not moved by the Waldensian slanders <note>The author is likely referring to a specific group of "Waldensian Respondents" who held views similar to the Reformed/Calvinist tradition regarding the Eucharist</note>, by which they sophistically distort the words "bodily" or "in a bodily manner" against our true meaning. They mock us with these ironic words: *Let him who can understand, understand* <note>original: *Qui potest capere capiat*; a reference to Matthew 19:12, used here by the opponents to imply that the Lutheran position is an incomprehensible absurdity</note>. For sounder minds, and those who possess a degree of sincerity, understand that there is no confusion or trouble in our position.

# NOTATIONS

In our time, the **Sacramentarians** <term>Sacramentarians: a term used by Lutherans for reformers, such as Zwingli or Calvin, who believed the bread and wine were only symbols or that Christ’s body remained only in Heaven</term> contend for a "spiritual presence." They set this in opposition not only to a perceptible and fleshly presence, but also to the true and substantial body of Christ. They deny that He is present here on earth with the bread of the Holy Supper. For this reason, those phrases of the ancient fathers—found in the **Apology of the Confession** <note>The *Apology of the Augsburg Confession* (1531), a foundational Lutheran document written to defend their faith against Catholic and radical reformer critiques.</note> and other writings—were brought back into use. This was done to show that the body of Christ is present in the Supper celebrated on earth not only according to its "power and efficacy" <note>The idea that only the *benefit* of Christ is present, rather than Christ Himself.</note>, but also according to its substance. It shows that His body is communicated to us not only spiritually through faith, but also "bodily"—that is, the very substance of the body itself is shared in the Holy Supper.

Since these points are plain and clear, we are not moved by the **Waldensian** slanders. They sophistically twist the terms "bodily" or "corporeal" against our intended meaning, and they mock us with those ironic words: *Let him who can understand, understand.* <note>original: *Qui potest capere capiat*; a quotation from Matthew 19:12, used here by the author’s opponents to suggest the Lutheran position is nonsensical.</note> Truly, those with healthier minds, and those who possess some honesty, understand that there is no confusion or difficulty hidden here.

# CONCERNING THE FIRST CHAPTER

<meta>catchword: [conjun]ctus</meta>

I have thoroughly reviewed the reasons and firm arguments concerning the **personal presence of Christ** <term>personal presence: the doctrine that the whole person of Christ—both His divine and human natures—is present, not just His spirit or power</term> in the Church and among the elect, which is being discussed here. Of this kind is the argument taken from the testimonies of Holy Scripture, in which **CHRIST** Himself promised that He would be present (Matthew 18:20; chapter 28, last verse; and John 14:18. Also Revelation 1:1 and chapter 3).

These testimonies are not to be understood "nakedly and simply" as referring only to the presence of Christ according to His Divine nature alone, or only regarding His "power and efficacy" <note>original: *virtutem & efficaciam*; the author is arguing against the view that Christ is only present through His influence, like the warmth of a distant sun, rather than being there Himself.</note> (which is all my **opponents** <note>The "Antagonists" refers to the Sacramentarians or Calvinists who argued for a purely spiritual presence.</note> acknowledge). This is proven by what **CHRIST** Himself preached in John 6 regarding the **eating of His flesh** <term>manducatio carnis: the sacramental eating of Christ’s body</term> and the **drinking of His blood**. He promises that in this way, He will be and remain in believers, and believers in Him. It was recently shown that the **orthodox Fathers** <note>The early Christian theologians of the first centuries after Christ, whom both sides in the Reformation claimed as authorities.</note> also understood these passages in this same sense.

Next, I proposed another no less evident argument based on the fact that He is present to the Church as **King, Priest, Emmanuel** <note>original: *Immanuel*; Hebrew for "God with us."</note>, **patron**, and **protector**, by reason of the office He administers according to both His divine and human natures. Since, therefore, it is rightly attributed to these same offices that He is present to the **Church militant** <term>Church militant: the Christian community currently living on earth, struggling against sin and temptation (as opposed to the "Church triumphant" in heaven)</term> on this earth, by what logic can it be said that this presence does not belong to Him according to both natures?

Another reason is touched upon by me afterward: that **CHRIST** is present to His Church according to that nature as well by which He is most closely **joined** <note>original: *coniun[ctus]*; the text cuts off here, but the catchword "ctus" indicates the word is "joined."</note> to us as our brother...

Therefore, they contend that Christ works all things simply "in the concrete" <note>referring to the person of Christ as a whole, but attributing the action only to one part</note> by reason of His **Divinity**. They are unwilling to acknowledge that in His **Royal office**, His **Priestly office**, and His **dominion** over all things, that same Divinity—through the **communication of operations** <note>the theological doctrine that the attributes and actions of one nature are shared with the other in the person of Christ</note>—effects all things in and through the **Human nature**, treating it as an inseparable, personal, proper, and divine instrument <note>original: "organum"</note>.

# REMARKS

<note>original: "NOTATIONES"</note>

With what faith and patience, then, could I or should I have endured those deserters, contrary to the command of the Holy Spirit? For by that command, every person is forbidden to desert the congregation to which they are joined, and is prohibited from leaving any room for an unnecessary schism <note>A formal split or division within a church body</note>. How could I also allow it that, by their terrible example, others might be provoked for a longer time toward a similar crime of desertion while I am still living? For by doing so, I would be sharing in the sins of others.

### IX.

Citing the words of my booklet in bad faith—as they usually do—they add their own inventions here: as if I wish to administer the Sacraments <note>The sacred rites of the church, such as Baptism and Holy Communion</note> to everyone indiscriminately, without any prior instruction or examination. Yet even the *Apology of the Augsburg Confession* <note>original: "Apologia Augustanæ Confessionis." A foundational document of Lutheran theology written in 1530</note> commands such preparation.

For their own formal words, which have already been set forth from their *Apology* <note>original: *Apologia*; a formal written defense of their faith</note> mentioned earlier, testify to the contrary. In these words, they explicitly set forth an exclusion and contend that the **Sacred Supper** <note>Holy Communion or the Eucharist</note> must be administered only to those who share in **CHRIST** through faith in Him, such as those who are the **Brothers and Sisters of CHRIST**, and they claim that these true Christians are to be found only in their own assembly. ...those committed to the **Augsburg Confession** <note>original: *Augustanae Confessioni*; the primary confession of faith for the Lutheran Church, which the author is defending</note>, as it is necessary for them to understand) they attack most fiercely with great vehemence of words, in a manner hardly becoming of a **Brotherly order** <note>A jab at the "Bohemian Brethren" (Unitas Fratrum), suggesting their behavior does not match their name</note>. ### CONCERNING THE THIRD CHAPTER

...cited, which was also expressed in my earlier writing in distinct words: Whether such external discipline is rightly considered a more essential part of a religion, or the sinew <note>original: *nervus*; the vital strength or binding force</note> upon which it depends? And, whether a congregation should be rejected or abandoned because it does not everywhere obtain—or cannot obtain—the discipline it desires, even while the Articles of true faith remain safe and intact? 

The Respondents cunningly disguise this status of the controversy, or at least touch upon it only in passing among other things. However, it is manifest that they hold tenaciously <note>original: *mordicùs*; literally "with their teeth"</note> to the affirmative view, as shown by the sentiment inserted in the Preface of their own *Confession*, by the public testimony of the matter itself, and by the listeners whom they have alienated from our own congregations. 

On the contrary, we who profess the **Augsburg Confession** <note>The primary confession of faith of the Lutheran Church, presented in 1530</note> constantly defend the negative position for several most grave reasons assigned in that same book of mine. To these I add this: that something may be lacking in discipline and its stricter observation with less danger than in the knowledge and profession of purer doctrine and the sincere handling of the **Sacraments** <note>Religious rites, such as Baptism and the Lord's Supper, considered as means of grace</note>. These latter things, by the testimony of the sacred oracles of GOD <note>The Holy Scriptures</note>, are uniquely necessary for salvation and are required before any other things. This cannot be said of external discipline and human works, even though my antagonists in their *Confessions* sometimes assert it and other times deny it, and repeatedly contradict themselves.

**IV.** The Respondents seem to falsely invent things about me, as if I believed that the administration of the **Sacraments** <note>Religious rites, such as Baptism and the Holy Supper, seen as means of God's grace</note> is legitimate and consistent with the example of **CHRIST** and His disciples when they are administered indiscriminately and equally to the ungodly—those who are the authors of manifest scandals, or convicted of the greatest crimes and do not perform **penitence** <note>original: *pœnitentiam*; repentance or the outward expression of regret for sin</note>—as they are to the godly who know **CHRIST**. 

For we by no means neglect this kind of discernment, nor do we admit just anyone to the use of the Sacraments in our churches without a proper Examination. Instead, where the situation requires it, we suspend them from that use, and we do not admit them until signs of repentance have first been observed.

This applies not only to the cause, merit, and effectiveness of works, but even to the necessity of their presence during the actual moment of <term>Justification: the theological act by which God declares a person righteous through faith alone</term>, insofar as that act is being considered. Thus, works that follow justification and faith, since they are its effect, can by no means be placed in the role of the <term>efficient cause: the primary agent or force that produces an effect; in this case, the author argues works do not "cause" salvation</term>.

### OBSERVATIONS

Matthew, Peter, Ambrose, and Martin—by the command and arrangement of **God** <note>original: "DEO"</note> himself—changed their former way of life in such a way that they were completely occupied with the single **office of the Ministry** <term>Ministerium: the formal religious service or office of a clergyman</term>. They administered this office with constant vigilance and for the salvation of the whole **Church** <note>original: "Ecclesia"</note>, and from then on, they set aside secular affairs.

On the other hand, the ministers of those **Brethren** <note>Referring to the Bohemian or Waldensian Brethren, who often worked manual jobs alongside their ministry</note>, although they may hold little sermons on the Lord's days—brief talks without a solid foundation, plucked without judgment from **postils** <term>postillae: books of pre-written sermons or commentaries used by less-educated preachers</term>, or sometimes simply read aloud—spend the rest of their time devoted to their own crafts and to handling secular business.

For this reason, in my booklet I added other arguments against the mixing of these different functions. These were based on the difficulty of the **ecclesiastical office** <note>original: "muneris Ecclesiastici"</note>, the necessary support of the **liberal arts** <term>artes liberales: the traditional academic subjects like grammar, logic, and rhetoric necessary for higher study</term>, and the study of doctrines which are absolutely essential for teaching correctly.

Therefore, if the **Respondents** <note>The opposing party in this theological debate</note> think that their ministers have been legitimately called to this type of office, why do they not order them to devote themselves hereafter to that same office and to the studies necessary for it, as would be proper?

Furthermore, I deny that one who is to be a **Theologian** <note>original: "Theologus"</note> should also practice **medicine** <note>original: "Medicina"</note> in such a way that they spend the greatest part of their time and care on it. This is because the theological calling is not only far superior because the soul excels the body, but also because he knows it requires much more study, reading, vigilance, and constant attention.

Hence, they wrongly cite my own example here; they will never be able to prove in any way that I [spent] a greater and more frequent...

# OBSERVATIONS.

III. They write that **poverty** often compels a **Minister of the Church** to necessarily devote some effort even to physical labors. I do not debate here whether they truly need so many Ministers—and especially the traveling preachers they use for sermonizing—or whether fewer men could be supported at less expense. Likewise, I do not debate whether **those Brothers** <note>The author uses "those Brothers" to refer to the opposing religious group, likely the Anabaptists or a similar radical sect</note> are merely pretending to perform the "labors of their hands" due to poverty—using a certain **monastic** simulation <note>original: "Monastica simulatione"; he suggests they are acting like monks who took vows of poverty to gain sympathy or status</note>—while they actually enjoy all their necessities quietly and peacefully (as one of their own associates has written). 

But I add only this: if there were any real learning in them that would qualify them to correctly lead an Ecclesiastical office, there would be no shortage of people willing to hire them for a fair wage and provide moderate sustenance. This would ensure that **Sacred studies** <term>studia Sacra: the academic study of scripture and theology</term> would not necessarily be hindered by outside chores and business. While we certainly do not approve if any Minister devotes himself to the luxury of banquets, or vain pleasures, and gambling—as they imply here—or if he indulges in other frivolities, it simply cannot be allowed that the readings and sacred duties (which must be attended to entirely and diligently) be hindered and confused by profane matters. One should not trade **literary and liberal arts** <term>liberales: studies "worthy of a free person," such as logic, rhetoric, and philosophy</term> for **manual and illiberal trades**.

Why have they wrapped in their own corruptions, or obscured, the principal points of Christian doctrine—as shown by others and by me—within their public Confessions? ### ON THE FOURTH CHAPTER

...will be more tolerable than by those unrefined, coarse, and ignorant simpletons <term>idiotis: In this context, not a slur on intelligence, but a technical term for uneducated laypeople lacking formal schooling</term>, who have been devoted from childhood not to noble and sacred pursuits, but to base, profane, and sordid crafts and affairs. This justice is divinely sanctioned in the Fourth Commandment of the Decalogue <note>In the numbering system used by the author, the Fourth Commandment is "Honor your father and mother," which was traditionally interpreted to include respect and proper provision for all authorities, including teachers and clergy</note>, which distinguishes the ranks of persons and offices in life by geometric proportion <note>A mathematical ratio where rewards are proportional to status, rather than a "simple" or equal distribution for everyone</note>, and assigns to each their appropriate place, honor, duty, and corresponding reward. Where this is not observed in common life, a confusion and destruction of ranks, duties, and rewards will necessarily be introduced, not without immense public disturbance.

XIII. They did this by summoning them at certain times of the year to the "synagogues" <note>The author uses this term here likely in a derogatory sense to refer to the Brethren's meeting houses</note> they maintain elsewhere. Sometimes they even did this within the city itself, in private houses, as I reviewed above in Note II regarding the second chapter of our disagreement. Finally, it can be understood from this that they can no longer deny what happened in previous years: they very frequently dared to administer the Word and Sacraments in secret corners, "running out" <note>original: "excurrendo"; a term used for itinerant preaching that bypassed the local parish system</note> to places where they had not been sent. 

Furthermore, their citation of that specific example is utterly ridiculous and foolish: namely, that among the Germans, those devoted to their studies <note>original: "literis operam dantes"</note> are employed for the exercise of preaching in villages and administering sacred rites. The reasoning in that case is entirely different. For such things are permitted to Students and Candidates of Theology, but certainly not to unlearned men <note>original: "idiotis"; refers to those without formal university training</note> or craftsmen. This is not done so that they may "put their sickle into another man's harvest" <note>A biblical metaphor (from Joel 3:13 or Revelation 14:15) used here to mean interfering in the work and territory of another established minister</note>, nor to entice listeners to themselves with the allurements of words to the insult of the Church and the ordinary Ministry of each place, nor to provide reasons for a treacherous defection to another segregated group; rather, it is done solely for the sake of practice and testing their abilities. ## CONCERNING THE FIFTH CHAPTER

[...antago]nists, I have proved: 1. From the sacred Scriptures <note>original: "sacris Instrumentis"; likely referring to the Old and New Testaments as the "instruments" of God’s revelation</note> of the Old and New [Testaments], by testimonies and examples, by which it is established that from the beginning in the Church, the Word and the Sacraments were observed together with the highest reverence, because they were held in equal rank, and were of the same authority and value. 2. From the nature and institution of the Sacraments themselves, which depend entirely upon the divine Word itself—as if from the command and promise of the almighty GOD or CHRIST the Lord—which must be grasped by faith. For since the promise is general, faith in it and the use of the Sacrament apply that promise to individual believers. 3. From the interpretation of Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian whose views on the "visible Word" of the Sacraments were central to Reformation thought</note>, that just as the connection of the Word and the Sacrament is indivisible, so also by reason of dignity and power, one is not greater or of less value than the other. 4. From the purpose or primary effect of the Sacraments, by reason of which a greater degree of the efficacy and consolation of the Holy Spirit <note>original: "Spiritus sancti"</note> is produced in the Sacraments than in the lone and bare Word, particularly when one has reached the point of temptations, the struggles of conscience, and the final spiritual agony. For in this way, those things which strike the eyes move the mind more than those which are perceived by the ears. 5. From the common [declaration] of our Churches, namely the Augsburg Confession <term>Augsburg Confession (Confessio Augustana): the primary statement of faith for the Lutheran movement, presented to Emperor Charles V in 1530</term>, which cites the authority of Augustine in support of the same opinion. 6. ### ON THE FIFTH CHAPTER

From the Response of the Bohemians <note>original: "Bohœmicorum"; referring to the Bohemian Brethren, a Hussite-influenced Protestant group whose "Confession" was a subject of much debate</note>, it will be possible to learn from its express words. III. *They contend that the Word is therefore to be valued more highly than the Sacraments because* GOD *wished it to be heard more frequently and above all else, and for that reason instituted feast days.* But indeed, did He not wish the doctrine concerning the Sacraments to be proposed at the same time within that same Word, and along with the other <term>Articles of religion|Fundamental points of Christian doctrine that define a church's faith</term>, and their saving fruit to be declared and practiced, even if their external use was not always performed? <note>The original Latin "actories" is likely a transcription error for "actu," meaning "in actual practice."</note> They add the example of CHRIST the Lord: *That He most diligently administered the proclamation of the Word, and taught long before He instituted the Holy Supper.*

However, they ought to have considered that the discussion here is not only about the Lord’s Supper, but also about Circumcision, and the Baptism which was substituted in its place; just as then both were in frequent use on both ordinary days and the Sabbath, besides the fact that the same Lord instituted the Holy Supper in such a way that it too should be celebrated frequently. Concerning the disciples of CHRIST they also add: *That He sent them into all the world with these principal commands, that they should teach and preach the* Gospel, *which...*

...and they themselves have done so faithfully. With that same logic, they add the following:

> *Shall we truly say that the Sacraments are diminished because the proclamation of the Word occurs and is practiced more frequently?*

The issue here is not whether it occurs or is practiced more frequently; rather, this is the <term>κρινόμενον|the central point at issue</term> <note>original Greek: krinomenon</note>: Whether the preaching of the Word, by reason of its dignity, power, and necessity, should be placed above the administration of the Sacraments. This is exactly what cannot be allowed, as it opens a window not only to the diminishing of the Sacraments but even to a profane contempt for them.

IV. They write:

> *If truth and faith, and all those things which ought to precede the use of the Sacraments, are not present in someone's heart, the Sacraments provide no benefit, because they do not find the very thing they were meant to confirm.*

But they cannot prove this way either that the Word must be preferred to the Sacraments in dignity, power, and necessity. For even if those things which must precede the use of the Sacraments are not present in a person’s heart without the preaching of the Word (at least where adults are concerned), the Word is not therefore to be valued more highly; rather, the Sacrament is equally sublime—

### ON THE FIFTH CHAPTER

<meta>catchword: V. Re</meta>

...ly worthy and useful, since one is perpetually included in the other. Nothing can truly and properly be called a **Sacrament** <note>original: "Sacramentum"</note> if its physical element, its divine mandate, and its promise—as well as the entire ritual action—are not contained within the **Word**. Here they also urge the point that an impressed or attached seal is of no benefit to an empty document <note>original: "diplomati"; referring to a legal charter or official letter</note> in which no words are written. We, on the contrary, and rather by inverting the argument, say: A document or written letters are not valid unless they have an impressed and attached **seal**. 

Hence it was recently stated that the Word (or the promise) is general, while faith and the use of the Sacrament apply that promise to individual believers. Likewise, a greater efficacy and consolation depend on the Sacraments than on the lone and "naked" Word <note>The term "naked word" (nudum verbum) refers to preaching that is not accompanied by the visible signs of the Sacraments</note>. 

Moreover, they indicate clearly enough in the following words that they are referring to those who are already adults. They suggest that adults, having been converted in their own time and place through the preaching of the **Gospel** <note>original: "Euangelij"</note>, attain faith from that preaching, so that in this way the Sacrament also offers its own fruit and efficacy. 

But they feel that this efficacy should not yet be understood in this way regarding **infants** <note>original: "infantibus"</note>. Indeed, they do not believe that infants are regenerated through **Baptism** and attain faith, since they are not capable of reason and cannot hear the preaching of the Gospel. Instead, they determine that children are eventually led to faith in their own time, once they have reached a more mature age, through the **Ministry of the Word**, as will be discussed later.

<summary>The author argues that while the Word contains the promise of God, the Sacraments act as the "seal" that validates and applies that promise to the individual. He also critiques the opposing view that infants cannot benefit from Baptism because they lack the reason required to hear the Gospel.</summary>

# ANNOTATIONS

<meta>catchword: VI. Scri</meta>

**V.** Those who respond to me, by misusing a certain saying of the Apostle <note>Likely referring to St. Paul's discussions on circumcision in Romans 2:25</note>, argue rashly against my assertion in the following manner: Circumcision benefited the pious Jews under the law, but it was a hindrance to the impious; therefore, the **Ministry of the Word** <note>original: "Ministerium verbi"; the formal preaching and teaching of the Scriptures</note> is more sublime and greater, and more necessary for salvation, than the **Sacrament**. Or they argue: **Baptism** in the New Testament—which has replaced **Circumcision**—benefits true Christians but is a hindrance to the false; therefore, the Word is to be preferred over the **Sacrament** in its dignity. 

But indeed, can one not also argue in this same way regarding the preaching of the Word itself? The Ministry of the Word benefits true Christians but is a hindrance to the false; therefore, should the **Sacrament** be preferred over the **Gospel** <note>original: "Euangelium"</note>? The same judgment applies to the examples they add. For many of those from the **Israelite** people whom **GOD** <note>original: "DEVS"</note> did not approve, and who were struck down in the desert, were not only circumcised but were also instructed by the Word. And yet, just as with circumcision, the Word was not useful or salutary for them. Thus, one cannot be preferred over the other for that reason. 

By a similar reasoning, not only **Baptism** but even the preaching of the **Gospel** conferred no salvation at all upon **Simon Magus** <note>A figure from the Book of Acts who was baptized but later rebuked by Peter for trying to buy spiritual power; used here to show that even "the Word" can be received ineffectively</note>. Therefore, by no means—based on utility or efficacy—can either the Word be considered greater and more excellent than the Sacrament, or the Sacrament than the Word, by drawing from sayings and examples of this kind.

<summary>The author refutes the argument that the Word is superior to Sacraments by pointing out that both are equally ineffective if received by the impious, using the example of Simon Magus and the Israelites in the desert.</summary>

### ON THE FIFTH CHAPTER

<meta>catchword: in pa/</meta>

**VI.** They write: "The **Institution of CHRIST** <note>original: "institutio CHRISTI"; the formal establishment of the sacrament by Jesus</note> sounds no differently. 'He who believes,' (says the Lord) 'and is baptized, shall be saved'; nor, on the other hand, does he say, 'He who is not baptized shall be condemned.' Instead, having first joined both—'He who both believes and is baptized shall be saved'—He adds afterward, 'But he who does not believe (as if to say, even if he were baptized in an external way) shall be condemned.'" <note>A reference to Mark 16:16</note>

From these points, they once again fail to prove that the preaching of the word is worthier and more useful than **Baptism**. For although in the second part of this passage the two are not joined as they were in the first—but with Baptism omitted, it is only said: "*But he who does not believe shall be condemned*"—it still does not follow from this that Baptism is thinner or more lowly than the Word. Rather, this must be understood as referring to a **Case of Necessity** <note>original: "casu necessitatis"; a theological doctrine stating that if a person truly desires a sacrament but is physically unable to receive it before death, God grants the grace of that sacrament regardless</note>, by reason of which those who are forced to go without Baptism are not condemned. 

For as **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), an influential early Christian theologian</note> writes in the fourth book of his work *Against the Donatists* <note>original: "contra Donatistas"; the Donatists were a schismatic sect that argued sacraments were only valid if performed by a "pure" minister</note>: "*Baptism is fulfilled when not a contempt for religion, but a moment of Necessity, excludes one from visible Baptism.*" 

It should also be noted that they argue this point in vain, as if we were suggesting that the **Sacraments** alone, without **Faith**, were sufficient for **Eternal Salvation**, where they quote: "*He does not only say 'he who is baptized,' etc.*" Next, those who respond will have to see by what reasoning their own **Gloss** <note>original: "glossa"; an interpretive explanation or commentary on a text</note>...

<summary>The author argues that while Mark 16:16 emphasizes faith, the omission of baptism in the clause regarding condemnation is intended to accommodate "cases of necessity" rather than to devalue the sacrament. Citing St. Augustine, the text maintains that baptism and faith are both vital, and the absence of the physical ritual only goes unpunished when it is physically impossible to receive.</summary>

# NOTATIONS.

[The explanation] placed in parentheses agrees with orthodox truth: *But he who does not believe (as if to say, even if he were baptized in an external way) shall be condemned.* <note>original: "Qui verò non crediderit (quasi dicat, Etiamſi externo modo baptiſatus fuerit) condemnabitur." A continuation of the commentary on Mark 16:16</note> But was not that other point also stated by **CHRIST** in the gravest words concerning the use of Baptism as necessary for salvation in John 3:5? *Truly, truly I say to you, unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of GOD.* Therefore, in the ordinary way—not separately or segregated and torn away from **Baptism**, but with it and through it—the **Holy Spirit** <note>original: "Spiritus sanctus"</note> works rebirth and salvation. Therefore, let these opponents consider whether, by the reasoning they use here regarding Baptism, they are not tearing apart the divine operation and this Sacrament, which are joined by an inseparable bond; and whether, by thus belittling Baptism, they can escape the errors of **Schwenkfeldianism** <note>The followers of Caspar Schwenkfeld (1489–1561), who emphasized the "Inner Word" and spiritual experience over external religious rituals and sacraments</note> and **Anabaptism** <note>A movement that rejected infant baptism, often arguing that the physical water is merely a symbol and that the Spirit acts independently of the rite</note>, since they continue to argue that faith, rebirth, and salvation are not conferred through external and visible means, such as the Word and the Sacraments.

### VII. The sayings of Luther which they object to in this place,
taken from a writing sent to them—stating namely that more weight is placed on the Word than on the Sacrament, etc.—he [Luther] set these things down at that time when he had scarcely emerged from the **Papacy** <note>original: "Papatu"; the Roman Catholic Church</note>. He wrote them in opposition to the **"work performed"** <term>opus operatum: the doctrine that sacraments are effective simply by the act of being performed, regardless of the faith of the recipient</term> of the **Papists** <note>original: "Pontificiorum"; referring to Roman Catholics</note>, who claimed that without faith and without any good movement from the one using it, the Sacraments of the New Testament justify and [confer] grace.

VIII. [No] <note>original: "Ne". This is likely a catchword, the first word of the following page, or a section marker.</note>

they pretend to bring. Therefore, we constantly condemn this kind of foul error, along with the **Apology of our Confession** <note>The *Apology of the Augsburg Confession* (1531) is one of the foundational symbolic books of the Lutheran Church, written to defend the faith against Catholic refutations.</note>, and we simply feel it is a **Jewish opinion** <note>In the theological language of this era, a "Jewish opinion" (opinio Iudaica) referred to the belief that performing a religious ritual grants God's favor automatically, regardless of the person's internal heart or faith.</note> to believe that we are justified through a ceremony, without a good motion of the heart—that is, without faith. # NOTES

VIII. So that the **Waldensian Response** in this chapter as well might not lack insulting attacks—besides the fact that they charge my *Examination* with malice and slander, and with a hatred of the truth detected in them—they play with my surname and call me **quarrelsome** <note>original: *rixosum*. This is a pun on the author's name, likely Polycarp Lyser, suggesting he is "Lyser the Liar" or "quarrelsome."</note>, because I noted corruptions and expressions in their **Confessions** that were alien to orthodox truth. 

But since the same thing happened to the prophets of **Jehovah** at the hands of the impious—to whom, because of the word of truth which was bothersome to them, the prophets were most hated and considered **men of quarrels**—this should not seem unusual to me either. They, however, not only intentionally neglect these points, but even bring forward arguments that are discrepant, or rather diametrically opposed to them. Thus, through an attack on my own position, they are actually attacking that same Confession, as will be made manifest from the reasons they provide below.

-># NOTES.<-

...than the ***Habrovanites*** <note>original: "Habrovanitis." # CONCERNING THE EIGHTH CHAPTER

VIII. It relates that many intelligent and pious men have correctly and in a positive light accepted the idea that they should establish a spiritual and effective presence of the body of **CHRIST** in the **Holy Supper**. We easily concede this regarding those who are of the same sort <note>original: "eiusdem... farinæ," literally "of the same flour." But they criticize us as if we were some kind of troublesome and restless men, by whom those matters are variously agitated.

Indeed, with what faith and truth can they write again that *they believe simply in the words of CHRIST, and do not depart from those things which the Evangelists teach and set forth, and which Saint Paul explains?* <note>original: "Se verbis CHRISTI simpliciter credere, & ab his non discedere, quæ Euangelistæ docent & exponunt, & D. Paulus explicat?"</note> For do not these sacred writers, as witnesses beyond all exception, teach with great consensus that **CHRIST** the Lord, in this His **Testament** <note>original: "Testamento." Therefore, it is a free choice for Christians to have images and monuments of past deeds, just as our own Apology of the Augsburg Confession indicates in Article VII and in the Treatise on Sacrifices, among other places.

Since, following the venerable <term>Martin Luther<note>The German priest and key figure of the Protestant Reformation whose views on religious art were more moderate than those of other Reformers like Zwingli or Calvin.</note></term>, the theologians of our tradition have discussed this at length, I now add only this very briefly: the preceding words, and those following which are connected with them, testify that it is not simply all images that are forbidden here, but those which are held as idols and which are worshipped. For the commandment immediately preceding—<note>original Latin: "Non habebis Deos alienos coram me"</note> "You shall have no other gods before me"—indicates that nothing should be made that is worshipped in the place of God, or alongside the true God. Likewise, the following phrase, <note>original Latin: "Non adorabis ea, neq; coles"</note> "You shall not worship them nor serve them," proves that the aim of this prohibition against images and <term>sculptures<note>Specifically "sculptilia," referring to carved or graven images.</note></term> is so that divine worship and honor are not granted to them. In the same chapter, verse 23, it is clearly indicated what kind of statues God strictly forbids to be built, where He says: <note>original Latin: "Non facietis Deos argenteos: nec Deos aureos facietis vobis"</note> "You shall not make gods of silver, nor shall you make gods of gold for yourselves." The words of Leviticus 19, verse 4, declare the same: "Do not turn to idols, nor make cast gods for yourselves; I am <term>Jehovah<note>A common Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton (YHWH), the personal name of God.</note></term> your God, etc." On other occasions, however, apart from adoration and idolatrous worship, God Himself allowed images, as is abundantly clear from the decorations in the <term>Tabernacle<note>The portable earthly dwelling place of God used by the Israelites from the Exodus until the building of the Temple.</note></term>, in the Temple of Solomon, and in the royal house and throne. Therefore, if all images were forbidden simply in or of themselves by the first commandment of the <term>Decalogue<note>The Ten Commandments.</note></term> or the words connected to it, God would by no means have left a place for them in the Tabernacle and the Temple, which were consecrated to Himself, and among the <term>Levitical<note>Relating to the tribe of Levi and the specific priestly laws and rituals of the ancient Israelites.</note></term> rites...

**IV.** In the following words, in which *the Respondents contend that the images which are tolerated in our Churches can be an incitement to idolatry and a stumbling block for those living now and for posterity,* they do nothing other than play with the <term>fallacy of the accident<note>A logical error where one argues from a special or accidental case to a general rule, or confuses an accidental property with an essential one.</note></term>. **V.** They abuse a saying of **Luther** in bad faith, playing a trick through the **fallacy of the qualified statement** <note>original: "fallacia secundum quid, ad dictum simpliciter"; a logical error where a statement that is true only under certain conditions is treated as if it were true in all cases</note>. The Respondents <note>original: "Respondentes"; the authors of the theological critique the author is answering</note> criticize this with the following words: *That what is heard without sin may also be painted without sin.* But in truth, these are not my words, but those of Doctor Luther <note>original: "D. Lutheri"; referring to Martin Luther, the German reformer</note>, which state the following: *Who does not see that, just as pious histories are recited without sin and even with benefit to the listeners, in this same way, for the sake of the unlearned <note>original: "rudes"; literally "the raw" or "unrefined," referring to the illiterate or those lacking formal theological education</note>, such histories can also be painted and sculpted, not only in private homes, but in public places, etc.* Since they therefore carp at Luther, it is no wonder that they do not spare me.

Regarding the fact that they indicate they reject images of **GOD** without distinction, I now add this: that neither I nor others—theologians of our Confession <term>Confession; a formal statement of religious belief, likely referring to the Lutheran Augsburg Confession</term>—are accustomed to approve those images of **GOD** the Father or of the Holy Trinity <note>original: "S. S. Trinitatis"; the Most Holy Trinity</note> if someone attempts to use them to outline or place before the eyes the essence of **GOD**, which is altogether infinite and incomprehensible. But truly, when they are depicted historically, according to the modes of revelation expressed in the Holy Scriptures, such as in Isaiah 6, Daniel 7, Matthew 3, etc...

<meta>This page continues the dedication to Lord John Spanovsky, moving from the mention of his patronage of a theological book to a defense of the Augsburg Confession. The text emphasizes the continuity of Lutheran doctrine with the earliest biblical teachings.</meta>

[you are] a true lover and a most fierce defender of the Confession. This is as pleasing to me as anything could be, since the *Augsburg Confession* <note>The primary statement of faith of the Lutheran Church, presented in 1530</note>, not only in all its *Articles*, but even (so to speak) in its very *points*, agrees excellently and clearly with the *Prophetic* and *Apostolic* doctrine. This doctrine is the only truly true and ancient one, because the *Son of GOD, our Lord JESUS CHRIST*, revealed it to the first *Fathers* and *Patriarchs* immediately after the fall of *Adam*, long before He assumed *Human nature*.

This is clearer than the midday sun from the *Prophetic* writings and prophecies. For I am now so certainly persuaded that if the *Prophets* themselves, and *CHRIST* Himself with the *Apostles*, had been present at that *Augsburg Synod* <note>The Diet of Augsburg in 1530, where the confession was delivered to Emperor Charles V</note>, they would not have brought forward or approved *Articles* different or discrepant from those which were printed in the first edition. This is true even though many "wise-men" <note>original: *sapientuli*; a mocking term for those who think they are more clever than the scriptures</note>, however many they are who think themselves too wise, do not agree with them in all things or in certain places. But I do not wonder at this; they will one day discover, to their own great misfortune, that each and every one of these *Articles* was most true. 

Thus, you act rightly, piously, and holily, *Noble Lord*, my friend to be reverently honored, in that you embrace each of these said *Articles* and [assent] to them from your heart...

# To the Reverend and Most Distinguished Man,
## Master JOHANN HEDERICUS, Doctor of Sacred Theology, governing the Church of GOD at Jihlava <note>original: "Iglaviæ," the Latin name for the city of Jihlava in the modern-day Czech Republic</note>, his beloved Lord and friend.

->GREETINGS IN CHRIST JESUS.<-

### Reverend Sir, Lord
and most beloved brother in CHRIST, I lovingly give thanks to your Kindness, because you have deigned to greet me with your learned and pious letters, and moreover you have sent over a little book, which I shall read with pleasure. I consider that you are performing an exceptionally good work, because you are openly showing to the Church of GOD the fanaticism and errors of the Waldensians <note>original: "VValdensium." While the Waldensians were a medieval movement, in this period the term was often used by critics to describe the "Unity of the Brethren" (Bohemian Brethren) in Bohemia and Moravia</note>, which are scattered far and wide not only through Bohemia and Moravia, but also through Poland and here in Prussia; and you warn the simpler folk to beware of them. GOD in turn will bless you, and I ask that you persevere vigorously by the grace of GOD in such a Confession <note>original: "Confessione," referring to a public declaration or statement of faith</note>, nor allow yourself to be frightened away by the threats of certain people. For He who commanded you to refute those who contradict and to stop their mouths <note>A reference to the biblical instructions for bishops in Titus 1:9-11</note> is greater than they are. The Devil is not put to flight, nor are his errors driven away, by keeping silent and turning a blind eye—

For the **Waldensians, Schwenkfeldians, Anabaptists** <note>These were radical Reformation groups. # ANOTHER [WORK] BY THE SAME AUTHOR, to be prefixed as a preface to the Waldensian Treatise on **OBLIGATIONS**, translated from the **Bohemian**, and now necessarily opposed to the most hateful "Negatives" of the Antagonists, chapter 2, Discrepancy Note 5, and chapter 4, Note 2, and others.

Greetings. <note>original: *S.*; an abbreviation for *Salutem*, the standard Latin greeting meaning "Health" or "Greetings"</note> You will wonder, and not without reason, kind and friendly Reader, that the style or phrasing of this writing does not savor of the language or the specific character of German expressions; and you will undoubtedly say that such obscure, confused, and unusual locutions can neither be read by the learned without offense, nor understood by the unlearned <term>Idiotis: from the Greek *idiotes*, referring here to laypeople or those not formally trained in scholarship, rather than a modern insult</term>. But indeed, if you look into the "Original" (as they call it) written in **Bohemian** <note>original: *Bohæmicè*; the Czech language</note> by the **Waldensians** <term>Waldensians: a proto-Protestant Christian movement founded in the 12th century; by the time of this text, they were often being compared to or integrated with Lutheran and Reformed traditions</term>, you will immediately cease to wonder. You yourself will recognize that I have not overstepped the bounds of a faithful **Translator** <note>original: *Interpretis*</note>, and that I have set forth many things more properly and skillfully than they were originally composed by them. I see that many things were set down obscurely and intricately on purpose, so that they might have loopholes for errors lurking secretly within. For if they wished to act with sincerity and declare their opinion openly, what would be the purpose, or what would be the need, to [wrap] the core <note>original: *cardinem*; literally "the hinge," meaning the essential point or pivot of an argument</note> of the passage or the matter under discussion so many times in such...

# FORMULAS OF OBLIGATIONS,
by which they bind themselves when being received into the Unity of the Bohemian Brethren <note>original: "Unitatem Fratrum Bohemicorum." God and the Church gave the right and power of calling <term>Ministers: formally appointed and ordained religious leaders</term> to those to whom the sheep of that Church have been entrusted and commended; and they, and no one else, must give an account of their <term>Stewardship: the responsibility of managing the church and its members, much like a manager overseeing a household</term> to God and men. Therefore, they cannot fail to seek out the straying sheep who wander into another <term>Fold: a metaphor for a specific church community or congregation</term>. ### VIII.
They act against <term>Scripture: the Holy Bible</term>, which commands that we do not desert our public congregations, lest the <term>Concord: the state of peaceful agreement and unity</term> and unity of the Church be torn apart—a subject about which <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258 AD) was a prominent Bishop of Carthage known for his influential writings on the necessity of church unity</note> Saint Cyprian wrote extensively. By doing this, the godly are divided into various <term>Sects: separate, often dissenting, religious groups</term>, the common defense of doctrine and the faithful is hindered, and the <term>Devil: the personification of evil and the enemy of the faith</term> can more easily overcome and uproot the Church by attacking its members one by one. For by Concord the Church grows; through discord it is scattered and extinguished.

### X.
The <term>Sacraments: sacred rites of the church, such as Baptism and Communion</term>, which are public and not private rites, they turn into a conspiracy and a plot of a few against the rest of those who hold the correct view.

### XI.
It necessarily follows that, since the Brethren are often far away from those places where they have few fellow believers, sick infants either die without <term>Baptism: the rite of admission into the Christian Church</term> or are baptized by the <term>Pastors: the local ministers or shepherds of a congregation</term> of those places. Since they therefore approve of that Baptism and consider it legitimate, yet steer their adults away from the use of the <term>Lord’s Supper: the ritual sharing of bread and wine, also called Holy Communion</term> and the preaching of the word, it follows that they value Baptism less than the Supper. This is despite the fact that the Sacraments are equal. In those matters where the public <term>Ministers: formally ordained church leaders</term> remedy their shortcomings and provide them with an excuse for their absence, they consider them legitimate Priests; but in other matters which are greater, they consider them deceivers, <note>original: "lupis & Mercenarijs," a reference to John 10:12 where Jesus speaks of the "hireling" who abandons the sheep when the wolf comes.</note> wolves, and hirelings. Yet the right to baptize belongs only to those who teach, and through Baptism an infant is grafted into that Church of which the baptizing Pastor is a Minister.

### XV. They harm the consciences of their own people.

For when the <term>Magistrate: a civil government official</term>, as was just said, forbids secret <term>conventicles: private, unauthorized religious meetings often held in secret</term>, and compels those who refuse to approach the <term>Lord’s Supper: also known as Communion or the Eucharist</term> with the rest of the community to sell their property; those who sell their goods and leave behind their sweet homeland, parents, friends, and so forth, do so with the greatest loss to their family estate. This cannot happen without pain, hatred, and the cursing <note>original: "execratione"</note> of those who expel them.

Let the Brothers <note>Referring to the leaders or members of the Bohemian Brethren</note> see how greatly those who agree with them might curse and pursue them with hatred when, for serious reasons, they eject the stubborn with great pain. And it often happens that such people, having been subjected to such great dangers, when they do not find among the Brethren what they had hoped for, later realize that they did not have sufficient reasons for the <term>desertion: the act of abandoning one's homeland or duties</term> of their country, their friends, their lands, and so on. Afterwards, in their hearts, they curse the Brethren by whom they were driven to these things.

Or it happens that they join with the rest of the people in attending sermons and <term>Sacraments</term>, and they abstain from the assemblies of their own Brethren, whom they once held to be the best and most sincere Christians. Instead, they join themselves with those very people they once considered heretics. This can by no means happen without the wounding of their conscience; indeed, it agitates them day and night. And then, soon enough, they are considered unworthy even of conversation by their former Brethren, treated as deserters, traitors of the truth, and servants of physical goods and of <term>unjust Mammon: a biblical term (from the Greek 'mamonas') referring to wealth or property, often implying it is a false god</term>, as people who have cast away faith and a good conscience.

### XVI. They cast themselves and their doctrine into danger.

For if a pious <term>Pastor: a local parish minister</term>, performing his duty alongside a pious <term>Magistrate: a civil government official</term>, were to come to their private assembly and inquire into the reasons for their clandestine meetings and their contempt for the public Ministry, and why they intrude upon another’s <term>calling: the authorized station or territory of a minister</term>; and if the Pastor were to examine them on the principal Articles of faith, some would be more silent than a fish <note>original: "pisce magis muti"; a Latin idiom for being completely silent</note>—especially the boys. These boys are often sent not only to villages, but even to cities where there are sometimes quite praiseworthy and learned Priests, even though these youths can often **SCARCELY DEFEND THE CATECHISM** <term>Catechism: a summary of religious principles used for instruction</term>.

Anyone who does not see how an ordinary Pastor could capitalize on these circumstances—strengthening the firmness of his own doctrine, magnifying the falsity of the Brothers (even if it were purer), and so confirming his own people in their opinion, while injecting doubt into the Brothers, bringing even true doctrine into contempt and hatred, and utterly embittering minds against the Brothers—is blinder than a mole <note>original: "Talpa magis cæcus est"</note>.
