# FROM THE ARTICLES OR PROPO-
## *sitions of John Wycliffe the Englishman, concerning*
### *the Lord’s Supper.* <note>original: "Cœna Domini"</note>

Just as John [the Baptist] was figuratively Elijah, and not personally: So the bread is figuratively the body of **CHRIST**, and not naturally the body of **CHRIST**. And that without any ambiguity, this is a figurative expression: *This is my body,* just like those words of **CHRIST**, *John himself is Elijah.* <note>Wycliffe argues that when Jesus said "This is my body," he was using a metaphor, just as he did when he identified John the Baptist as the prophet Elijah (Matthew 11:14).</note>

Likewise, the body of **CHRIST** is not substantially in the <term>Sacrament of the Altar</term> <note>Another name for the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> if one considers the body of **CHRIST** according to its own nature: but [the bread] is there substantially, corporally, and dimensionally, in the manner of the host, according to its own nature. <note>Wycliffe is arguing for "remanence"—the idea that the substance of the bread remains bread even after consecration, rather than disappearing and being replaced by the physical flesh of Christ.</note>

Likewise, the Sacrament of the altar is naturally bread and wine: Sacramentally it is the body of **CHRIST**.

Likewise, just as **CHRIST** is at the same time **GOD** and man, so the consecrated host is at the same time the body of **CHRIST** and true bread: because it is the body of the Lord in figure, and true bread in nature: Or, which sounds the same, it is true bread naturally, and the body of **CHRIST** figuratively.

Likewise, once the material and formal predication is established, a Catholic must grant habitual predications in the Scriptures, such as, *The seven cows are seven years,* <note>A reference to Joseph’s interpretation of Pharaoh’s dream in Genesis 41:26, where the cows represent years, not literally becoming them.</note> And to the Cor-

# ON THE SAME SUBJECT TO HIS LORD FATHER, FROM HIS SON <note>The "same subject" refers to the anagram from the previous page, where "Agreement" (Consensio) was identified as a core trait of Johann Hederich’s character.</note>

*That Agreement should rightly be thought pleasing to the pious,*
*Which stands upon the eternal Word of GOD.*
*When every unlawful thing and schism <note>original: "schismate"; a formal division or separation within a church body.</note> is removed,*
*A single faith resounds among all Christians.*
*Thus, by fostering the same doctrines with a steady heart,*
*Christ Himself nourishes us, joined together in Him.*
*But if the Rule of the Sacred Word <note>original: "Regula Verbi"; the principle that the Bible is the sole authority for faith and practice.</note> should be violated,*
*If foul schisms tear apart the holy flock:*
*Then a harmonious opinion is falsely boasted, and in vain*
*Does a deceptive coat of paint mask false doctrines.*
*Falsely is a more severe Censure <note>original: "Censura"; this likely refers to the strict moral discipline and "Ecclesiastical Censure" for which the Bohemian Brethren were well-known, which the author here critiques as superficial.</note> of testing*
*Outward behaviors boasted of, as they are accustomed to celebrate.*
*While pride, scorning others, holds dominion, clinging*
*To their hearts, and a great lust for evil boils within.*
*Thus, if the foundations of a solid faith are lacking,*
*Certain ruin lies beneath the remaining parts.*
*So a company torn apart by various reasonings at last*
*Does not head toward the stars by the single path of Christ.*
*Minds are drawn from there into tangled errors,*
*Which nothing but a thousand disasters can follow.*
*Hence, reverend Father, since true agreement is in your heart,*
*You would desire all deceit to be far away.*
*Let it not move you at all that a spiteful tongue*
*Falsely says that you love trivial quarrels.*

For any mind conscious of what is right laughs at such things,

  Hiding at home like a tortoise. <note>original: "testudinis instar." This classical metaphor suggests that a man of Jan's character could not stay safely tucked away in private life while the state required his service.</note>
Therefore, King **Ferdinand**, welcomed into your court,
  He diligently presided over his assigned duties. <note>Ferdinand I (1503–1564) was King of Bohemia and Hungary, and later Holy Roman Emperor.</note>
Among those distinguished by their ancient nobility,
  He did not allow himself to hold the lowest rank.
But he proved his deeds and his devotion to his Lord,
  And from that time, the King’s generous favor was his constant companion.
And when his loyalty became apparent to others, behold!
  He was placed at your side, **Maximilian**. <note>Maximilian II (1527–1576), Ferdinand’s son, who would later succeed him as Emperor.</note>
When you lent your allied right hand in battle against the treaty-breaking French,
  While **Charles** was waging war. <note>Emperor Charles V was frequently at war with the French king, Francis I, over territories in Italy and the Low Countries.</note>
When arms had settled these conflicts and peace was restored,
  He returned to his former post at the King’s wish.
And guarding this position with his customary virtue,
  He remained a willing servant of the King for some years more.
Until, at last relieved of this duty, he followed
  The blood-stained camps of grim Mars. <note>original: "Martis... castra." Mars is the Roman god of war; the poet uses this to signal Jan’s transition from civil service to military life.</note>
While the Prince of **Saxony** and the **Landgrave** waged new wars
  Against the supreme Monarch of the Empire. <note>This refers to the Schmalkaldic War (1546–1547), a conflict between the Catholic Emperor Charles V and the Schmalkaldic League, an alliance of Protestant princes led by John Frederick I of Saxony and Philip I of Hesse.</note>
Later, when he had learned the arts of warfare through long practice,
  He was present in arms in many different places.
Whether he bore weapons to defend the borders of the Empire,
  Or when the plague of rebellion needed to be suppressed.
Thus, he also assisted with a strong hand in defending the fortress
  Of **Győr**, which stood against the incursions of the Turks. <note>original: "RHABAM... Geticis." Győr (German: Raab) was a vital defensive outpost in Hungary. "Getae" was a classical name used by Neo-Latin poets to refer to the Ottoman Turks.</note>
Thus, as a fierce knight, he marched with various nations
  Against the rebellious **Hungarians** who rose against you, **Ferdinand**. <note>original: "HVNNOS." The poet uses "Huns" to refer to Hungarian rebels or factions who opposed Habsburg rule during the ongoing territorial and religious disputes in the region.</note>

<summary>This page describes Jan Spanovský's entry into the royal court of Ferdinand I and Maximilian II, followed by his transition to a distinguished military career fighting the French, Protestant rebels in the Schmalkaldic War, and the Ottoman Turks.</summary>

Bb 5

While the King tamed these men by force and compelled them to obey,
->All the men endured great dangers.<-
For various citadels and many a rampart,
->Strong by both art and the nature of their site, offered up battle.<- <note>The "art" refers to military engineering and fortifications, while the "site" refers to the natural defensive advantages of the terrain.</note>
These places, therefore, could not be overcome by a mild war,
->Nor could such a great matter be carried out without bloodshed.<-
Nevertheless, no less for that, through the great courage of his men,
->The King subdued them, drawing the conquered under his scepter.<-
Then also the noble virtue of **Jan Spanovský**
->Shone forth, proving the noble lineage of his race.<- <note>original: "generis nobile stemma." Spanovský is demonstrating that his personal bravery matches the high status of his family tree.</note>
Intrepid, because he was shielded by his own inner strength,
->He resisted every attack with a steady foot.<-
Inflicting wounds on others, he brought his own limbs back home
->Uninjured, once the enemies had been defeated.<-
Perhaps around this time, there departed from the King’s court
->The Lord who bears the name of the **Rose Mountain**,<- <note>original: "De Roseo Monte." This refers to a member of the House of Rosenberg (Rožmberk), the most powerful noble family in Bohemia, whose emblem was a five-petaled red rose.</note>
So that he might take up the management of his own estates,
->Which fortune had offered him upon the death of his ancestors.<-
This Lord joined Jan to himself and brought him back to his own roof,
->In which Jan had lived for a long time before as a boy.<- <note>It was common for young nobles to be raised as pages or squires in the households of higher-ranking lords.</note>
Having successfully employed Jan’s service for many years,
->The Lord cherished him with affection for his supreme loyalty.<-
At last, the fates brought the day on which, by a lawful treaty,
->He was to become the husband of his wife.<-
Therefore, hurrying home, he renounced the customs of the court,
->And prepared himself for such sacred rites through pious vows.<-

And, with **GOD** guiding him, he leads away the daughter of a Spanish father,
->*Born of a Silesian mother,*<- <note>original: "Iberi... Schlesia." This refers to his wife, Anna of Tovar, whose father was Spanish and mother was from Silesia (modern-day Poland/Czechia).</note>
**ANNA OF TOVAR**, from the famous lineage
->of Barons,<-
Whose noble family tree flourishes
->*among the SPANIARDS.*<-
Joined to her, he fathered a modest offspring of both sexes,
->*future members of the kingdom of GOD.*<-
Whom he instructed by his own example and advice,
->*drawing their tender hearts toward every pursuit of virtue.*<-
(For precepts are of no use if examples contradict them;
->*he who teaches by example, teaches best.*<-)
And above all, he imbued their minds with the love of piety,
->*and educated them in the Holy Scriptures.*<-
Of which he was so diligent a searcher, that to him,
->*nothing else was of greater or prior importance.*<-
From this, by the grace of **GOD**, he made such great progress
->*in the Christian religion,*<- <note>original: "Christisona," literally "Christ-sounding" or "proclaiming Christ."</note>
That he was able to offer sound judgment on all points
->*where controversy pricks or troubles the mind.*<-
For this reason, he embraced the Ministers of the Word with such love,
->*those who hand down the sacred dogmas with faithful trust:*<-
So much so that his *Citadel* was a *Sanctuary*
->*for many exiles, and a refuge for the pious in their misery.*<- <note>original: "Arx illius esset Asylon." This suggests Spanovský used his fortified estate as a safe haven for religious refugees, likely Protestants fleeing persecution.</note>
On the other hand, he pursued heretics and blasphemous
->*enemies of CHRIST with such zeal, making no pretenses:*<-
That he would rather have the whole world set against him,
->*than to have sought to please an insincere man.*<-

--- Page 447 ---
<meta>This page continues the biography of Jan Spanovský. The previous page concluded by describing how Spanovský turned his home into a sanctuary for religious exiles and pious people in need.</meta>

From this point, he bore three years of suffering with a patient heart,
->**Pious and like the martyrs.**<-
And when the care of physicians offered no cure,
->*He was restored only by the hope of divine help.*<-
And although he was overwhelmed by heavy torments,
->*Nor did even a brief hour give rest to the poor man,*<-
Yet he was not broken in spirit, nor did he ever cease
->*To hold firmly to his hope in the Lord.*<-
Nor did he diminish his study or his fervent zeal
->*When Religion needed his aid for its defense.*<-
Rather, constant in spirit, he advanced against the enemies
->*Who attack the teachings of Christ with secret warfare.*<- <note>original: "occulto... Marte." This uses the name of the god of war, Mars, to signify a hidden or spiritual conflict.</note>
Who do not fear to shamelessly violate the <term>Sacrament of the Supper</term> <note>Referring to the Eucharist or Holy Communion. In the religious conflicts of the time, groups like the Waldensians were often accused of "violating" this sacrament by denying the physical presence of Christ in the bread and wine.</note>
->*By denying the words of Christ our GOD.*<-
Who carry wolfish hearts beneath sheep’s clothing,
->*And swell up, puffed with feigned Religion.*<-
Who deceive the simple-minded with pretenses, while they claim
->*That they too love the teachings that harmonize with Holy Scripture.*<-
(I depict in their true colors the <term>Waldensian</term> <note>A reformist religious movement. In the context of 16th-century Bohemia, this label was often applied to the "Unity of the Brethren," whom critics like Spanovský viewed as heretical.</note> bands,
->*Whom terror and error drive hither and thither in various ways.*<-)
Their hidden frauds and deceits he uncovered to everyone
->*By the light of the Divine Word.*<-
He even invaded their exposed camps with his writings,
->*Taking up public arms against these known enemies.*<-
In this, **HEDERICH** was the standard-bearer, who, relying on the Divine Will,
->*Was the first who did not fear to approach his enemies.*<- <note>original: "Hedericvs." This likely refers to Christoph Hederich, a contemporary scholar or theologian who collaborated with or inspired Spanovský in his polemics.</note>
He was the first to approach, and the first to carry away the <term>palm</term> <note>A symbol of victory or triumph.</note> after the battle,
->*A prize he merited by the goodness of his cause.*<-

<summary>This page describes Jan Spanovský’s three-year period of illness and his fierce intellectual defense of orthodox Christian sacraments against the Waldensians. It highlights his collaboration with the scholar Hederich in publishing polemical works.</summary>

--- Page 448 ---
<meta>This page continues the praise of Jan Spanovský, specifically focusing on his deliberate and consulted approach to religious defense and his eventual passing. The previous page ended with him uncovering the "frauds and deceits" of his theological opponents.</meta>

This joyful victory emboldened Jan Spanovský
->**To stand more firmly against these men.**<-
Lest he should seem to you to have rushed headlong into arms,
->**Or to have prepared for war with a rash hand:**<-
Know that he weighed these matters for quite a few years beforehand,
->**And saw that God was his authority.**<-
Indeed, he even sent to foreign shores to consult
->**Famous men of sincere religion.**<- <note>This refers to Spanovský seeking counsel from leading Protestant theologians abroad, likely in Germany or Switzerland, to ensure his religious stance was doctrinally sound.</note>
He consulted teachers of the sacred word from every side,
->**Whom the German lands foster in their learned schools.**<- <note>original: "Teutona terra." Referring to the Holy Roman Empire, which was the intellectual heart of the Reformation.</note>
He stood by their judgment, and performed all things
->**By their encouragement; he held these men as his guides through those battles.**<-
Therefore, with alacrity (certain that these wars were waged for Christ),
->**He seized his enemies with vigor,**<-
Sparing nothing of his wealth, his zeal, or his labor
->**Until he saw them defeated by the Word of God.**<-
When he had obtained this, he thought he had lived long enough,
->**And he returned his soul to Christ and passed away.**<-
You, pious posterity, and kinsmen of noble blood,
->**See that you imitate the virtues of such a great man.**<-
Thus the splendor of your lineage will grow, as will your glory,
->**And there will always be a writer to celebrate you in song.**<-
And lest you be in doubt as to what time he left the earthly
->**Sphere, seeking the stars: hold fast this couplet:**<-
That father of his country, Jan Spanovský,
->**Died at the very time of your birth, O Christ.**<- <note>This final couplet is a <term>chronogram</term>, a popular 16th-century word puzzle. The capitalized letters in the original Latin (I, L, V, C, M) function as Roman numerals which, when added together, provide the year of his death: 1585. The text indicates he died on Christmas Day.</note>

<meta>This page continues the commemoration of the Bohemian nobleman Jan Spanovský, specifically describing the physical memorial—a portrait—he commissioned for his local church. # ON THE PORTRAIT OF THE MAGNIFICENT Lord JOHANN SPANOFSKÝ of Lylau the Elder, Lord of Pacov <note>original: "Patzauu." A town in the Vysočina Region of the modern-day Czech Republic.</note> in Bohemia, etc. Placed by himself in the Parish church there as an epitaph, two years before his blessed departure from this earth.

*When the court was too much under the Boleslavian sect,* <note>original: "Secta Boleslaviensis." Likely referring to religious factions centered in Mladá Boleslav, a significant center for the Bohemian Brethren, though the mention of "monks" suggests a Catholic influence Spanovský opposed.</note>
->*Which follows monks and favors the camp of the girdled ones,*<- <note>original: "Cinglica castra." A reference to the "Cingularii" or "Girdled ones," often a nickname for Franciscan friars due to the knotted cord (cingulum) they wore.</note>
*And no hero cared by what pious means false dogmas*
->*could be avoided,*<-
*Near these very places, I, Spanovský, sought from you,*
->*My Doctor Hedericus, your counsel and your zeal.*<-
*This came forth in writings, and I confess it was spread throughout the world*
->*at my expense; I refuse to keep the truth silent.*<-
*Let the Holy Church know this throughout these lands:*
->*Let he who is wicked finally cease to be wicked.*<-
*Thus, this image represents not only my face*
->*or my body, but also the very thoughts of my mind.*<-

# ON THE PORTRAIT OF THE REVEREND AND MOST RENOWNED MAN, Lord JOHANNES HEDERICUS, Doctor of Sacred Theology, placed closely at the side of the former.

*What you, O Hero, sought with holy zeal*
->*and with the love of piety, I, Hedericus, have written.*<-
->GOD willed it.<-

<note>This text highlights the partnership between the "Sword" (the nobleman Spanovský) and the "Pen" (the theologian Hedericus). It emphasizes that Spanovský’s religious reforms were not merely political, but based on the scholarly work he funded and Hedericus authored.</note>

<summary>This page contains the inscriptions for two memorial portraits in the church at Pacov: one of Jan Spanovský and one of his theologian, Johannes Hedericus. The verses celebrate Spanovský's role in funding and promoting Reformation theology against local monastic influence.</summary>

--- Page 450 ---
<meta>This page concludes the inscriptions related to the portraits of Jan Spanovský and his advisor, Johannes Hedericus. It continues the poem begun on the previous page, where Hedericus reflects on his duty to the church and the spiritual purpose behind the physical memorial.</meta>

God, the Word, and a just calling <note>original: "vocatio justa." In a Reformation context, this refers to the legitimate internal and external call to serve the church.</note> alike demanded this, 
    as did a mind devoted to the flock of Christ.
Because I have so often felt the wrath of enemies from that source, 
    all the honest deeds I performed were met with deceit.
I entrust this to Christ, whom no one can deceive, 
    and whose words can never lead the faithful astray. 
Not through force, but by the Word <note>original: "Verbum." This emphasizes the Lutheran and Reformed conviction that the Bible, not secular power or ecclesiastical hierarchy, holds ultimate authority.</note> does this prevail; 
    for the truths that are suppressed 
    will only shine with greater light the more they are weighed down.
Thus, from this [portrait], you may see not only the face I bore 
    in my fragile body, but also the very nature of my soul.

->F I N I S.<-
